chapters.title: Chapter 5: Market Microstructure and Execution Mechanics

lessons.title: Colocation, Latency, and the Race to the Top of the Book

body.text: When price cannot separate two market makers, because the tick is binding or because every desk has already converged on the same fair value, the only thing left to compete on is who gets their message to the exchange first.

markDefs.definition: The practice of placing a trading firm's own servers physically inside, or immediately adjacent to, the exchange's own data centre, so that the fibre-optic cable distance, and therefore the time, between the firm's system and the matching engine is as short as physically possible.

children.text: as a paid facility: any trading member willing to pay for rack space and a direct cross-connect can place its own servers inside the same data centre that houses NSE's matching engine. This is fundamentally a physics problem before it is a technology one. A signal travelling through fibre-optic cable moves at a large but finite fraction of the speed of light, so a server sitting a few metres from the matching engine reaches it measurably faster than a server sitting in a different part of Mumbai, and dramatically faster than one sitting in a different city altogether. No amount of clever software closes a gap created by physical cable distance.
The Latency Stack: Where Time Actually Goes
The total time between something happening in the market and a market maker's response reaching the exchange is made up of several distinct pieces, and colocation only shrinks some of them.

body.caption: Where latency comes from, and what actually reduces each piece

cells: A price or trade update travels from the exchange to the firm's server
The firm's own pricing logic decides how to react to the new data
Faster hardware and more efficient software, independent of location
The firm's resulting order travels back to the exchange
Colocation, again by minimising cable distance
The exchange itself processes and matches the incoming order
Not controllable by any individual trading member

body.text: Colocation only attacks the transmission stages. A colocated firm running slow, inefficient pricing logic can still lose a race to a firm sitting further away but making its decision faster, which is exactly why serious market making operations invest in both physical proximity and computational speed rather than treating either one as sufficient alone.

children.text: Why This Matters Most Exactly Where Chapter 2 Said It Would

Chapter 2's lesson on tick size explained that when a contract is tick-constrained, every market maker is stuck quoting the same bid and ask, so competition shifts entirely to queue position under price-time priority. Speed is what wins that competition. The same logic applies immediately after a scheduled announcement, from Chapter 4's final lesson: in the seconds after an RBI decision or a company's results are released, every market maker is racing to reprice before someone faster trades against a quote that is now stale relative to the new information. Colocation and low-latency infrastructure do not create an edge out of nothing; they let a market maker actually capture the edge that price-time priority and event-driven repricing already make available to whoever gets there first.
Speed-Based Adverse Selection: A New Way to Get Picked Off

markDefs.definition: Losses a market maker takes when a faster participant trades against its quote after the quote has become stale relative to new information, but before the market maker's own system has had time to cancel or update it, purely because of a speed disadvantage rather than any difference in what each side actually knows.

children.text: Chapter 4 covered adverse selection as a problem of information: a market maker cannot tell whether the trader on the other side simply knows more about the underlying's true value. There is a second, related but distinct problem worth naming clearly:

. Here, both sides may have access to exactly the same public information, for instance a futures price that just ticked. But if a market maker's cancel-and-replace message takes a few extra milliseconds longer to reach the exchange than a faster participant's incoming order, that faster order can trade against the market maker's now-outdated quote before it has a chance to update. Nobody involved knew anything the other did not; one side was simply faster to act on public information that had just changed.

columns.label: Information-Based (Chapter 4)
points: The other side genuinely knows something about fundamental value that the market maker does not
Priced in through the spread itself, using tools like PIN and VPIN
Cannot be fixed by being faster; the information gap is the problem
Concentrated around results, policy days, and other genuine news

columns.label: Speed-Based (This Lesson)
points: Both sides have access to the same public information; one side simply acted on it first
Priced in through infrastructure investment, not through the quoted spread alone
Directly reduced by colocation and faster decision logic
Concentrated in the milliseconds right after any price-moving update, large or small

children.text: The Economics and Regulation of Colocation Access in India

In principle, colocation access in India is open to any trading member prepared to pay for it, rather than restricted to a closed list of firms. That does not mean the resulting playing field is automatically level, since firms still differ enormously in how much they invest in engineering, hardware, and network optimisation beyond simply renting rack space. Fair and equal access to colocation and to exchange data feeds has also been the subject of real regulatory scrutiny in India: NSE faced a significant SEBI investigation, widely covered in Indian financial media through the second half of the 2010s, into allegations that some trading members had obtained preferential or earlier access to its colocation facility and tick-by-tick data feed compared to others.

body.text: This lesson describes the NSE colocation access episode only at a high level, since the specific findings, penalties, and settlement details evolved over several years of proceedings and are best verified directly from SEBI's own published orders rather than from a summary in a course like this one. The broader point that matters here is durable regardless of those specifics: equal, fair access to colocation and data feeds is a live regulatory concern, not just an engineering one, precisely because of how much a speed advantage is worth in a tick-constrained, price-time-priority market.

body.title: Diagnosing a Picked-Off Quote
body.scenario: A market maker's bid on a Bank Nifty option is hit by a large sell order less than ten milliseconds after the underlying futures price ticked down. The market maker's own system had already begun the process of lowering its bid in response to that exact futures tick, but the incoming sell order reached the exchange first.
body.prompt: Is this loss best explained as information-based or speed-based adverse selection, and what would help reduce this specific kind of loss in the future?
body.modelAnswer: This is speed-based adverse selection: both the market maker and the incoming seller were reacting to the same public futures price move, and the market maker was not out-informed, it was simply out-run in the milliseconds after the tick. Reducing this kind of loss requires attacking the latency stack directly, through colocation to shrink the transmission time for the cancel-and-replace message, and through faster decision logic to shrink the time between seeing the futures tick and sending the updated quote, rather than through anything that would help with information-based adverse selection, such as widening the spread based on an event calendar or a VPIN reading.

body.title: What Colocation Does and Does Not Fix
body.question: According to the latency stack in this lesson, which of the following is NOT directly reduced by colocation?
options: The time for market data to travel from the exchange to the firm's server
The time for the firm's own pricing logic to decide how to react
The time for the firm's resulting order to travel back to the exchange
Both of the transmission stages, to and from the exchange
body.explanation: Colocation shrinks physical cable distance, which directly reduces the two transmission stages, market data arriving and orders being sent back. It does nothing for how long a firm's own pricing logic takes to decide what to do with that data; that stage depends entirely on the firm's own hardware and software, independent of where its servers are physically located.

points: Colocation places a firm's servers physically close to the exchange's matching engine, minimising the fibre-optic cable distance and therefore the time data has to travel
Total latency has four parts: market data transmission, decision time, order transmission, and exchange matching time; colocation only shrinks the two transmission stages

Speed matters most exactly where Chapter 2 identified tick-constrained quoting, and exactly when Chapter 4 identified event-driven repricing races, because both situations turn on who reaches the exchange first
Speed-based adverse selection is a distinct problem from Chapter 4's information-based adverse selection: both sides may share the same public information, with one side simply acting on it faster
Colocation access in India is open to any paying trading member, but has also been the subject of real SEBI regulatory scrutiny over fair and equal access to the facility and to exchange data feeds

Together, this lesson and the previous one on order types complete the practical execution toolkit; the remaining lesson in this chapter turns to the exchange-side safeguards, circuit filters and price bands, that constrain how far any of this can move prices in a single session
